sections.title: What your accounting invoice must show
sections.body: A professional invoice for financial services must clearly separate different types of work. Your client needs to know exactly what they are paying for, especially when their own accounts must reflect these costs accurately. You must state the specific financial period the work covers. If you are billing for January bookkeeping in February, the invoice must note that the service relates to January. You also need to separate your professional fees from any disbursements. If you paid a company registry fee on behalf of your client, list this cost separately from your time so it is not taxed as your revenue.

sections.title: How accounting and bookkeeping work is billed
sections.body: Accounting practices typically use a mix of fixed fees and hourly billing. Monthly bookkeeping and payroll are usually billed as a fixed monthly fee for a strictly defined scope of transactions. Annual compliance work, like end-of-year accounts or tax filings, is often billed upon successful submission. When a client needs help outside this agreed scope, such as a deep dive into cash flow problems or a loan application, you bill this as hourly advisory work. You can create these documents quickly using our free invoice generator at /tools/free-invoice-generator to keep your billing cycle moving.

sections.title: Getting paid for your professional services
sections.body: Accountants and bookkeepers often face late payments despite managing other people's money. To protect your cash flow, set clear payment terms from day one. Many practices require a direct debit mandate for fixed monthly retainers, ensuring payment clears on the first of the month. For large annual compliance jobs or historical cleanup work, it is standard to request a deposit before you begin reviewing the ledger. If an invoice goes unpaid, stop all advisory work and pause any upcoming filings until the balance is cleared. Send polite but firm reminders the day after the due date.

faqs.q: How should I bill for client disbursements?
faqs.a: Disbursements are costs you pay on behalf of your client, such as official registry fees or specific software subscriptions. You should list these on a separate section of your invoice. This proves to the client that you are simply passing the exact cost along without adding a markup, and it keeps your own revenue figures accurate.

faqs.q: When do I invoice for annual compliance work?
faqs.a: Most accounting practices bill for annual tax filings and end-of-year accounts immediately upon completion and filing. However, some firms divide the estimated annual cost into twelve equal parts and add it to the monthly bookkeeping retainer. This smooths out cash flow for both you and your client throughout the financial year.

faqs.q: How do I handle out-of-scope advisory work?
faqs.a: Your engagement letter must define exactly what your fixed monthly fee covers. When a client asks for cash flow forecasting, loan application support, or complex tax structuring, you must flag this as out-of-scope immediately. Bill this extra work at your agreed hourly advisory rate and list the specific hours worked on your invoice.

faqs.q: Should I charge a deposit for new clients?
faqs.a: Yes, especially for historical cleanup work. When a new client brings you months of messy ledgers, the scope of work is often unpredictable. Charging a deposit of up to fifty percent before you begin reviewing their files protects your time if the client decides to abandon the process halfway through.
